Originally serialized weekly in Le Petit Vingtième from August 4, 1938 to August 10, 1939 under the working title 'Tintin en Syldavie,' the 1939 first album edition represents the crowning pre-war culmination of Hergé's black-and-white Bande Dessinée architecture before the 1947 62-page full-color redraw.

Narratively and politically, Le Sceptre d'Ottokar marks the decisive maturation of European sequential art into urgent geopolitical satire. Conceived in real time as Nazi Germany annexed Austria in the 1938 Anschluss, Hergé constructed two complete fictional Balkan states—the constitutional monarchy of Syldavia and the expansionist fascist dictatorship of Borduria, whose Iron Guard conspirator Müsstler fuses Mussolini and Hitler in plain sight. Through an ingenious narrative device—an illustrated Syldavian tourist brochure woven directly into the comic's pages—Hergé anchored a taut espionage thriller around the theft of King Ottokar IV's sceptre while introducing one of comics' most beloved recurring figures, Milanese opera diva Bianca Castafiore.

Aesthetically, the 106-page 1939 album exemplifies the clarity and architectural discipline of Hergé's Ligne Claire ('clear line') method: uniform ink line weights, meticulous European architectural and aviation documentation, kinetic silent chase sequences, and deadpan visual timing. Unlike American newsprint comic books of 1939, Casterman produced Le Sceptre d'Ottokar as a substantial hardcover book bound with a red cloth spine (dos toilé rouge), dark blue endpapers, an A7 back cover listing, and a small pasted-on front cover illustration (petite image collée) framing the Syldavian Pelican arms.
